title: Arcane Knockout
text: 3D wizard-duel arena game built with Unity 6 (C#), inspired by the Warlock custom map from Warcraft III. Online multiplayer, Windows build 0.0.9 (Oct 20, 2026). It was migrated to Unity 6 from an earlier prototype.

title: Arcane Knockout — What it is
text: There is no health bar. Every hit raises your Instability, so the next push throws you farther. The last wizard standing wins while the platform crumbles into the lava. Between rounds players spend gold in a shop. Arenas include a grassy island and a volcanic lava arena that collapses during the match.

title: Arcane Knockout — How it works (code architecture)
text:
Engine: Unity 6 (6000.6.5f1), C#, Mono backend.
One runtime assembly (ArcaneKnockout.Runtime, ~410 types, ~3.6k methods) organized into Gameplay, Net, Core, Arena, Rendering, UI, Audio and Input namespaces.
Gameplay in C#: MatchController, CombatMath, SpellClashRules (elemental spell clashes), ElementalStatus, bots (BotBrain, BotPersonality, BotShopper, GridNavigation), shop, titles and mastery.
Networking: online sessions with snapshot frames and a history buffer (NetFrame, NetFrameHistory), LAN room discovery and a relay/NAT-punch transport (NorayTransport), on Unity Netcode/Transport packages.
Procedural arena: platform graph and collapse planner (PlatformCollapseDirector, CollapsePlanner), procedural props.
Stack: Unity 6, C#, Unity Input System, ProBuilder, Unity Netcode/Transport.

title: Arcane Knockout — How it was built
text:
Role: Lian built the game logic and code — rules, combat, Instability, AI bots, shop, input, networking and builds — using an AI-assisted workflow. The art, textures and 3D models were AI-generated; visual scene design and 3D modeling were not part of this role.
AI-assisted workflow: development was driven with AI coding agents using written decision records, status/handoff docs and per-version delivery notes; every change was specified, implemented, then verified.

title: Architecture — Flow
text:
1. CLI (cli.py) parses commands and builds the pipeline from stickman.toml (config.py, validated, secret-free).
2. Orchestration (flow.py) takes an exclusive OS lock on the project for the whole run, pulls the next topic from the topic bank (bank.py), and records progress in a job manifest/journal (manifest.py). A crash releases the lock; the next run resumes the active job without consuming another topic.
3. Pipeline (pipeline.py) runs the stages:
script: scriptx/ generates a structured JSON script (scenes → visual concepts) via the configured LLM provider, validated against assets/script-schema.json; scriptx/gates.py enforces word budget and image density before any spend.
voice: voice/ synthesizes per-scene audio (Edge TTS default); voice/preflight.py checks measured duration.
align: word timestamps (Edge word boundaries or local faster-whisper) map concepts to time ranges (timeline.py).
stills: stills/runner.py estimates calls, checks the durable budget ledger, batches generation and caches images by (job, prompt, refs, provider, size, quality) + PNG hash.
compose: render/composer.py builds an FFmpeg filter graph with camera motion, crossfades, overlays (render/overlays.py), SFX and BGM ducking (bgm.py), then loudness-normalizes.
verify: verify.py probes the output and writes technical-check.json; thumbnailx.py builds the thumbnail.
4. Results are copied to deliveries/<id/.

title: Architecture — Design decisions
text:
Fail closed on cost: provider calls are gated by --live, by explicit provider choice (no implicit fallback) and by hard image caps. Every attempt is counted before it runs.
Providers behind small interfaces (providerbase.py, /base.py, /factory.py) so tests inject doubles and new services are easy to add (see docs/EXTENSIONS.md).
Idempotent stages with content hashes so re-runs reuse work.
No credential handling: Codex authentication stays inside the official CLI; API keys come only from environment variables.

title: How it was built
text:
🇪🇸 Español
This document explains why Codex Stickman Pipeline exists, how each stage works and the engineering decisions behind it. For the module map see ARCHITECTURE.md.

title: How it was built — The problem
text: Explainer videos ("stickman" / whiteboard style) are slow to make by hand: write a script, record a voice, draw or generate one image every few seconds, sync everything and edit. Most of that is repeatable. The goal was a single command — stickman run — that turns a topic into a finished 1080p MP4 with a thumbnail and caption, while keeping cost predictable and every run reproducible.

title: How it was built — Stage by stage
text:
Input → Output: Key idea.
topics file → next topic: Exclusive OS lock + job journal: a crashed run resumes the same topic instead of consuming a new one.
topic → JSON script (scenes → visual concepts): LLM output validated against script-schema.json; quality gates check pacing, word budget and image density before any paid call.
script → per-scene audio: Edge TTS by default (no key); ElevenLabs or any HTTP TTS behind the same interface; measured-duration preflight.
audio → word timestamps: Edge word boundaries or local faster-whisper; timeline.py maps each concept to a time range (~1 image / 12 s).
concepts → images: One batched generation call; durable budget ledger; cache key = job + prompt + refs + provider + size + quality, plus PNG hash.
images + audio → MP4: FFmpeg filter graph: camera motion, crossfades, overlays, procedural SFX, background music with ducking, loudness normalization.
MP4 → report: ffprobe checks (streams, duration, loudness) written to technical-check.json; 480p copy and thumbnail.

title: How it was built — Design decisions
text:
1. Fail closed on cost. Nothing paid runs without --live. Providers are chosen explicitly — no silent fallback to a paid API. Image calls are estimated and counted against a ledger before they run, so two runs cannot overspend together.
2. Small provider interfaces. Script, voice and image providers sit behind providerbase.py / factories. Adding a service is one class; tests swap in doubles.
3. Idempotent, resumable stages. Content hashes and a manifest let a re-run reuse finished work after a crash or a tweak.
4. No credential handling. Codex authentication stays inside the official CLI; API keys come only from environment variables. A release secret scanner is part of the test suite.
5. Offline demo path. A procedural-image + test-tone render works with zero accounts, so anyone can verify the FFmpeg path in minutes.
6. Own assets. Sound effects are procedurally generated; bundled music and fonts carry their licenses in THIRDPARTYNOTICES.md.

title: How it was built — Testing
text: pytest -q runs fully offline with test doubles for every provider: 94 passed, 2 skipped. Coverage includes topic-bank locking, config validation, provider contracts, script schema, pacing and budget gates (including a two-run budget race), image caching, the FFmpeg render path, output verification and the secret scanner.

title: How it was built — Workflow
text: Built in Python as a CLI-first tool, iterating with AI coding assistants: each change was specified, implemented, then checked by the test suite and by rendering real videos and inspecting the technical report. Real-run failures (overspending risk, crashes mid-job, pacing that felt too slow) became gates and tests rather than manual rules.

title: How it was built — What I'd do next
text: Vertical 9:16 output, more voice/image providers and a small web dashboard — see the Roadmap in the README.

title: 🎬 Codex Stickman Pipeline
🎬 Codex Stickman Pipeline — Why this project
text:
Faceless explainer videos take hours of manual work: writing, illustrating, recording, timing and editing.
This project automates the whole chain from a single topic line. It was designed and built by the author as an open-source project.
Key engineering ideas:
Stage-based pipeline (script → voice → align → stills → compose → verify). Every stage is idempotent and can be re-run on its own.
Pluggable providers behind small interfaces: LLM/image (Codex CLI with your ChatGPT login, OpenAI Images API, any OpenAI-compatible HTTP LLM), voice (Edge TTS, ElevenLabs, generic HTTPS TTS) and alignment (Edge word boundaries or local faster-whisper).
Cost safety: hard caps on image calls per video, pre-spend estimates, a durable cross-project budget ledger, no implicit retries, and no silent fallback to paid providers. Remote calls need an explicit --live flag.
Resumable & concurrent-safe: a topic bank with OS-level file locks, a job journal and content-addressed image caching, so a crash resumes without spending quota again.
Quality gates: JSON-schema script validation, word-budget/pacing checks before any spend, and a post-render technical report (duration, loudness, streams).
Broadcast-style render: 1920×1080 @ 30 fps master, Ken Burns camera motion, crossfades, overlays, SFX, music ducking (sidechain) and a −14 LUFS loudness target, plus a 480p copy and an auto-generated thumbnail.

title: 🎬 Codex Stickman Pipeline — Features
text:
Structured JSON scripts (scenes → visual concepts) with a target length (default 5.5 min, ~145 wpm).
About one new illustration every 12 s, generated in batched calls with a consistent minimalist style.
Edge TTS by default (no API key); ElevenLabs or any HTTPS TTS optional.
Scene and concept cuts aligned to the spoken words.
Camera motion, crossfades, captions/overlays, SFX and background music.
master.mp4 (1080p), 480p copy, thumbnail, script, caption with credits, metadata and a technical report.
Queue topics, run --batch N, resume after interruptions.
Procedural demo render plus a pytest suite that needs no network or API keys.

title: GlosSub — Architecture & how it was built — Pipeline
text: extract (FFmpeg, selected track → 16 kHz mono) → transcribe (MLX Whisper, word timestamps, hallucination filters) → segment (pauses, punctuation, length, duration) → translate (LLM in batches with context, validation and retries) → align (optional, LLM links phrases across languages) → render (ASS with colors, SRT, JSON). Each stage's result is cached and reused. Both a CLI and a local FastAPI web UI drive the same pipeline.

title: GlosSub — Architecture & how it was built — Modules
text:
CLI: Typer commands to run the pipeline, render, manage the cache and serve the web UI.
Pipeline: stage orchestration, restart from a given stage, force recomputation, skip if cached.
Stages: extract, transcribe, segment, translate, align, layout, render.
Providers: transcriber and translator interfaces; MLX Whisper and OpenAI-compatible LLM implementations.
Prompts for translation and alignment kept outside the code.
Pydantic models for words, cues, alignment groups and jobs.
Web: FastAPI server with a static UI, loopback by default, with path validation.

title: GlosSub — Architecture & how it was built — How it was built
text:
1. Spec first: a written plan and a decisions document that every implementer, human or AI coding agent, follows.
2. Assumptions checked on real data before building on them (word timestamps, structured JSON from the LLM).
3. Hardware-driven choice: on an Apple Silicon Mac, transcription uses MLX Whisper.
4. Milestones measured on a real sample episode.
5. AI-assisted workflow: implementation driven with AI coding agents using written briefs and handoff notes; Lian defined scope, reviewed results in the player and steered fixes.

title: GlosSub — Architecture & how it was built — Lessons learned
text:
Batch size matters: larger alignment batches produced truncated JSON in testing, so smaller batches were used.
Translation-length guards had to be set per language, because valid Japanese→Spanish output is much longer than the source.
Fill color reads better than colored outlines for the aligned words.

title: GlosSub — learn languages by watching series
text: GlosSub helps people learn languages by watching series. It captures and understands the audio with Whisper, an LLM translates it and generates the subtitles, and then it aligns the words between the original and the translation (color-coded) so learners understand the translation better. Technically, it is a bilingual subtitle generator with cross-language alignment: a command-line and local web tool (Python, FastAPI) that turns videos into bilingual subtitles. It uses FFmpeg to extract audio, Whisper to transcribe with timestamps, and a configurable LLM to translate the dialogue and, optionally, link fragments across languages. It exports ASS with color-coded correspondences, plus SRT and JSON, and reuses intermediate results through caching. Video is processed locally; text may be sent to an external provider depending on the configuration.

title: GlosSub — learn languages by watching series — What it's for
text: Language learners watching real video see the original line and its translation together. In the ASS output, matching words or phrases can share the same color, so the learner sees which part of the original corresponds to which part of the translation. Optional romaji for Japanese.

title: GlosSub — learn languages by watching series — How it works
text:
1. Extract: FFmpeg converts the selected audio track to 16 kHz mono audio for speech recognition. Input must be a format FFmpeg can read.
2. Transcribe: on Mac, MLX Whisper produces the dialogue with word-level timestamps, with filters that discard some likely hallucinations.
3. Segment: words are grouped into subtitle cues using pauses, punctuation, length and duration, which decides what text appears together and for how long.
4. Translate: cues are sent in batches, with context, to a configurable LLM over an OpenAI-compatible API. Responses are validated and retried; translation is not guaranteed to be complete, and untranslated cues can remain, flagged as low confidence.
5. Align (optional): the LLM links words or phrases of the original to the translation. This is meaning alignment shown as colors, not audio sync (timing comes from the transcription), and it can be partial.
6. Export and reuse: ASS (bilingual layout, colors when aligned), SRT (plain text, no colors) and JSON (structured data). Intermediate results are cached so stages are not repeated on the same material.

title: GlosSub — learn languages by watching series — Engineering story
text: The interesting part is the orchestration: transcription, segmentation, contextual translation, bilingual alignment and rendering, each as a separate stage with validation of LLM output and reuse of cached stage results.

title: GlosSub — learn languages by watching series — Privacy and security
text:
Video and audio are processed locally. Translation and alignment send text and context to the configured LLM endpoint; if that is a cloud provider, the text leaves the machine, and cost depends on the provider.
The local web UI binds to loopback by default and validates file paths. It has no authentication; it is a local tool, not meant for public exposure.
The API key is read from environment variables. LLM output is treated as untrusted and validated before use.

title: GlosSub — learn languages by watching series — Known limits
text:
The cache key does not include every processing option; changing some parameters (for example model or audio track) may reuse earlier results unless recomputation is forced.
Transcription is set up for MLX Whisper on Mac; other platforms are not verified.

title: GlosSub — learn languages by watching series — Sample run (one episode, not a guarantee)
text: On one sample run with a 23.7-minute Japanese episode: 253 of 254 cues were translated and 227 of 254 were colored by alignment (688 alignment groups). These numbers describe that run only and do not measure translation accuracy.
